newsitem.title: USA: Babbitt signs plan to release wolves in U.S. West.
newsitem.headline: Babbitt signs plan to release wolves in U.S. West.

text.p: Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt Tuesday signed off on a plan to re-introduce the endangered Mexican gray wolf into Arizona and New Mexico despite protests from ranchers, a source in his office said.
Babbitt formally approved a recommendation made Dec. 19 by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.
The decision is still awaiting the signature of Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman and Raymond Fatz, deputy assistant secretary of the Army, according to the source.

Under the plan, three family groups of wolves, each consisting of an adult pair and their offspring, would be released on public lands in the Apache National Forest in eastern Arizona within the next year.

The wolves, a subspecies of the North American gray wolf, would be allowed to wander into the forest and the adjoining Gila National Forest in New Mexico, providing nearly 7,000 square miles of habitat for the species.
Environmental groups hailed the news and stressed the importance of returning the Mexican wolf to the wild soon.
Only 148 Mexican wolves survive, all in captivity.
The administration's decision to release the Mexican wolf follows earlier decisions to reintroduce wolves to Yellowstone National Park and central Idaho.
Environmental groups are also pressing for release of wolves in their original habitats in Adirondack Park in New York and in Olympic National Park in Washington.

Defenders of Wildlife welcomed the decision and said it would pay ranchers for any verified livestock losses to wolves through its $100,000 Wolf Compensation Trust. The first wolves could be on the ground as early as November or December.
If wolves move beyond the designated recovery area onto private or tribal lands, they will be removed unless the land owners or managers want them to remain, the source said.
Additional family groups would be released each year over the next three to five years until there was a self-sustaining population of 100 wolves in the wild, the source said.
Under the plan, livestock owners would be allowed to kill wolves seen attacking livestock on private land.

Mexican wolves once roamed the mountains of the southwest and the range extended from Mexico City to southern Arizona, New Mexico and Texas. The last verified sighting of a live Mexican wolf in the wild was in 1980 in Chihuahua, Mexico.
Most of the wolves were killed by the 1930s after the government and ranchers launched aggressive programmes to hunt and trap them beginning in 1915.

The last wolves were eradicated by the early 1970s. Five wolves were trapped in Mexico in the 1970s. Their offspring include 120 of the 148 wolves now in zoos, sanctuaries and other facilities in the United States and Mexico.
Ranchers and farm organisations in New Mexico and Arizona oppose the plan, claiming that wolves pose a major threat to livestock. They have vowed to challenge the plan in court.
